summary.text: A 66-year-old male first presented to a local dental hospital with ulcers of the gingiva and bilateral buccal mucosa for one month that did not resolve with dexamethasone and lidocaine patches. Over the next 6 months he developed skin ulcers, sore throat, dysphagia and scalp blisters, and was referred to the authors hospital.

Immunological tests for anti-bridging protein 1, anti-bridging protein 3 and anti-BP-180 were negative, while C-reactive protein and hematological tests were within normal limits. A thigh blister showed subepidermal blisters with lymphocytic infiltrate. Laryngoscopy showed nasal, nasopharyngeal and epiglottic lesions with normal vocal cords, and immunofluorescence was positive, leading to a diagnosis of mucous membrane pemphigoid.

Oral methylprednisolone 1.0 mg/kg/day was started with methotrexate and tofacitinib citrate; tofacitinib citrate was halted after 2 weeks because of low back pain. After one month he reported significant relief, methotrexate was stopped and methylprednisolone was tapered to 10 mg/day, with laryngeal lesions resolved, occasional small skin blisters and no signs of recurrence at one year, although Table 1 lists relapse.

summary.text: A 50-year-old female with no significant medical history presented with 2 months of unexplained rhinorrhea and intranasal adhesions. A rhinotomy found extensive nasal erosions and ulcers, but nasal obstruction and rhinorrhea persisted, adhesions reformed after one month, and oral ulcers, skin blisters and ulcers and a pharyngeal foreign body sensation followed.

Dermatology biopsies of lower extremity and oral blisters, dynamic laryngoscopy and oral mucosal pathology showed subepidermal blisters, purulent secretions, crusting and nasopharyngeal stenosis, with linear IgM and IgA on direct immunofluorescence. Mucous membrane pemphigoid is stated for all four patients in the abstract.

Oral methylprednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/day gave no significant improvement after one week, so methotrexate 10 mg/week and then immunoglobulin 400 mg/kg/day were added, with rituximab also named in other sections. Remission followed one week of immunoglobulin, with maintenance methylprednisolone 0.3 mg/kg/day, no recurrence of nasal stenosis or epistaxis, and topical halometasone alone after 4 months, while Table 1 lists relapse.

summary.text: An 80-year-old female presented with severe dyspnea and laryngeal stridor, having undergone a tracheotomy 6 months earlier, and sought evaluation for removal of the cervical endotracheal tube. Fiberoptic laryngoscopy showed collapsed and adhered left nasal alae, purulent secretions in the right posterior nostril, annular vocal cord contraction and a relatively narrow glottis, with an unobstructed tracheostomy opening.

A pemphigus or pemphigoid condition was suspected and she was referred to dermatology, where examination, pathology and immunofluorescence confirmed mucous membrane pemphigoid. Dermatology recommended oral methylprednisolone 1.5 mg/kg/day; after 20 days of treatment her condition improved and the laryngeal lesions had not progressed, and the dose was tapered stepwise to 0.2 mg/kg/day.

She was evaluated for decannulation 3 months after maintenance therapy began, and no episodes of dyspnea were reported during the 6-month follow-up period. The source does not state whether the tube was removed.

summary.text: A 58-year-old female presented with a pharyngeal foreign body sensation and a persistent cough lasting 2 months, with no significant past medical history. Vonoprazan for suspected pharyngeal reflux disease did not relieve her symptoms, and laryngoscopy and CT showed nodular hyperplasia and thickening and narrowing around the left epiglottic fold, with later sore throat and dyspnea.

Follow-up laryngoscopy showed nasopharyngeal scar-like changes, soft palate adhesions with a small fissure, and irregular elevations of the epiglottis and ventricular bands with unaffected vocal cords, and oral ulcers and conjunctivitis followed. Consultation suggested mucous membrane pemphigoid, and oral mucosal biopsy and direct immunofluorescence showed subepithelial splitting and linear IgG and C3 deposition.

Oral methylprednisolone 0.4 mg/kg/day with methotrexate for 3 months controlled her condition and laryngeal lesions resolved. Methotrexate was stopped and the dosage was reduced stepwise, with no evidence of recurrence after 6 months, although Table 1 lists relapse.

article_limitations: The 17 published cases in the literature review and Table 2, and the pooled literature statistics, are not patients of this series; they are not individuated and no facts were recorded for them.
Patients are numbered by first mention including the abstract, which names the second, third and fourth patients before Case 1 appears, so p1 is Case 2, p2 is Case 3, p3 is Case 4 and p4 is Case 1.
The abstract sentence that one patient required a tracheotomy for severe dyspnea does not label the patient and was not assigned.

Table 1 gives Relapse as the outcome for Cases 1 to 3 without a time point, while the text reports no recurrence at the end of follow-up (Case 3: no recurrence of nasal stenosis or epistaxis); because the relapse is not placed in time the pair is recorded as an ambiguity, with the Table relapse review only and the text statements kept.

Table 1 prints Rhinorrhagia where the Case 3 text says rhinorrhea, Dermal division where the Case 1 text says subepithelial splitting, and After tracheotomy as the Case 4 initial symptom; none is reconciled.
Rituximab for Case 3 appears in the abstract, Table 1 and discussion but not in the case narrative; no dose or timing is stated.
The Case 1 dosage reduction sentence does not name the drug and mixes per-kilogram and absolute doses; recorded as printed.
The Case 3 text cites Supplemental Video 1 but the source declares no supplement or video asset; the video is unavailable media, not viewed or reviewed (complete, flagged), and no facts come from it.
The Figure 1 flow chart prints 115 retrieved records while the methods text says 113; the printed values are pixel content only and no patient fact depends on them.
Figure 7 is cited in the text as panels A to C but the image is a single unlabelled panel.
Figure captions describe immunofluorescence images as electron microscope images; this is caption wording only.
The abstract tracheotomy sentence is attributed by the abstract to the fourth patient, but the case text gives no indication for that tracheotomy; the stated reason (severe dyspnea) is not assigned.
